posts.title: The Afronauts ★★★ Royal Court Theatre | Nov 14 - Dec 19, 2026
posts.description: In 1960, former soldier, teacher and anti-colonial activist Edward Makuka Nkoloso established what he called the Zambia National Academy of Science, Space Research and Philosophy. As Zambia approached independence in 1964, he announced that his country would enter the international space race and reach the Moon before either the United States or the Soviet Union. His quixotic quest attracted the support of a group of young Zambians and the bemused attention of the international press. His motivations and intentions were open to a variety of interpretations. Was this the folly of a megalomaniac, a satire on the space race as an arena for the ambitions of the world's leading powers, or a genuine dream and a call for African people to aspire to a future beyond their present circumstances? In his "true-ish" retelling of this story, playwright Ryan Calais Cameron offers little insight into this central question, although the ending seems intended to be inspirational. posts.title: Nine Night ★★★ Kiln Theatre | Nov 12, 2026 - Jan 9, 2027
posts.description: Nine Night is the traditional Jamaican wake, observed during the nine nights following someone's death. It is both a time of mourning and a celebration of the deceased person's life, bringing family, friends and the wider community together. This ritual provides the backdrop for playwright Natasha Gordon's affectionate portrait of three generations of a family who gather to celebrate the life of the unseen Gloria. Gordon has a fine ear for dialogue, and the play is full of terrific lines. She also has a gift for creating recognisable, convincingly human characters whose foibles and family tensions will resonate with audiences. Llewella Gideon is hilarious as Auntie Maggie, the judgemental and interfering relative we have all encountered, while Gary McDonald is pitch-perfect as Uncle Vincent, whose true love may have slipped away. posts.title: Eurotrash ★★★★ Young Vic | Nov 13, 2026 - Jan 9, 2027
posts.description: The trope of a young man taken on a comic and educational journey by an older woman is hardly new. Eurotrash begins on familiar ground, recalling such antecedents as Travels with My Aunt , Auntie Mame and Harold and Maude . However, Christian Kracht gives the formula a distinctive purpose, using it semi-autobiographically to explore his relationship with his mother while also offering a fascinating allegory of European history. The drug-addled, drunken Mother, who hoards her fortune in Switzerland and is herself a product of the Nazi era, becomes emblematic of a continent that has showered the wider world with both excrement and money, while dominating it and drawing it into its political and military affairs since the colonial era. Her ineffectual artist son, Christian, in turn represents a contemporary European generation that loves its ancestors, is somewhat in awe of them and remains haunted by their legacy.
